title: What training does the EU Display Screen Equipment Directive require for computer users?
description: What Article 6 of Directive 90/270/EEC requires for training workers who use display screens, when it is due, and how it links to workstation analysis.
shortAnswer: The EU Display Screen Equipment Directive (Council Directive 90/270/EEC) requires that every worker who habitually uses a display screen as a significant part of normal work receives training in use of the workstation before starting that work and whenever the organization of the workstation is substantially modified. Article 6 also requires information on all safety and health aspects of the workstation, including the results of the employer's workstation analysis, break planning, and eye test arrangements.
keyTakeaways: Article 6(2) sets two training triggers: before a worker starts display screen work, and whenever the workstation's organization is substantially modified.
Only workers who habitually use display screen equipment as a significant part of their normal work are covered by the directive's definition of worker.
Article 6(1) requires information on all safety and health aspects of the workstation, in particular measures taken under Articles 3 (analysis), 7 (breaks) and 9 (eyesight).
Workers are entitled to an eye and eyesight test before starting display screen work, at regular intervals, and when they experience visual difficulties, at no additional cost to them.
The directive has applied since December 31, 1992; national laws transpose it and may add detail.
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National labor inspectorates enforce the transposing laws; the European Commission monitors transposition; the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) publishes guidance
appliesTo: Employers whose workers use display screen equipment at a workstation
Workers who habitually use display screen equipment as a significant part of normal work
Workers' representatives with a safety and health role
Managers who plan work routines and approve workstation changes

sections.heading: What is the EU Display Screen Equipment Directive?

blocks.text: The Display Screen Equipment Directive is [Council Directive 90/270/EEC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:01990L0270-20190726) of May 29, 1990, which sets minimum safety and health requirements for work with display screen equipment. It is the fifth individual directive under the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), whose provisions apply fully alongside it. Article 11 required Member States to bring their national laws into force by December 31, 1992.

The directive defines display screen equipment broadly as "an alphanumeric or graphic display screen, regardless of the display process employed". A workstation is the whole assembly around it: the screen, keyboard or input device, software, peripherals, document holder, chair, desk, and the immediate work environment. As at November 2026, the consolidated text shows only two amending acts, neither of which changes Article 6: Directive 2007/30/EC, which removed the national reporting provisions, and Regulation (EU) 2019/1243, which allows the Commission to make strictly technical amendments to the Annex by delegated act.

sections.heading: Which workers does the directive cover?

blocks.text: The directive covers only workers who habitually use display screen equipment as a significant part of their normal work. Article 2(c) defines a worker for this purpose as any worker under the Framework Directive "who habitually uses display screen equipment as a significant part of his normal work".
The directive does not define "habitually" or "significant" in hours, so national laws and guidance usually fill that gap. Article 1(3) excludes six categories of equipment entirely:

items: drivers' cabs or control cabs for vehicles or machinery
computer systems on board a means of transport
computer systems mainly intended for public use
"portable" systems not in prolonged use at a workstation
calculators, cash registers and equipment with a small data or measurement display required for direct use of the equipment
typewriters of traditional design of the "typewriter with window" type

blocks.text: The portable systems exclusion is narrow. It removes only portable systems that are not in prolonged use at a workstation, so a laptop used for long periods at a desk falls within the directive's scope.

sections.heading: What does Article 6 require for information and training?

blocks.text: Article 6 splits the duty into information under paragraph 1 and training under paragraph 2. Both apply on top of the Framework Directive's general information and training duties in Articles 10 and 12.

Under Article 6(1), workers "shall receive information on all aspects of safety and health relating to their workstation", in particular on the measures applicable to workstations implemented under Articles 3, 7 and 9. In all cases, workers or their representatives must be informed of any health and safety measure taken under the directive.

Article 6(2) is the training duty. It reads: "every worker shall also receive training in use of the workstation before commencing this type of work and whenever the organization of the workstation is substantially modified". The directive does not set a refresh interval, so periodic retraining is a matter for the risk assessment and national law. A substantial modification can include a new desk layout, a move to new software that changes how the work is done, or a change to the work environment, such as lighting, that alters glare.

blocks.title: Training in use of the workstation
blocks.text: The phrase is specific. Generic posture slides do not show that a worker can adjust their own chair height and seat back, position the screen to avoid reflective glare, use a document holder, or ask for a footrest, all of which the Annex requires the workstation to allow.

sections.heading: Which other duties should the training explain?

blocks.text: The training should explain the three linked duties Article 6(1) names: workstation analysis, breaks, and eyesight protection. Each gives the worker a right or a reporting route that only works if they know about it.

items: **Workstation analysis (Article 3):** employers must analyze workstations to evaluate safety and health conditions, "particularly as regards possible risks to eyesight, physical problems and problems of mental stress", and remedy the risks found.
**Daily work routine (Article 7):** the employer must plan activities so that daily screen work "is periodically interrupted by breaks or changes of activity".

**Eyes and eyesight (Article 9):** workers are entitled to an appropriate eye and eyesight test before starting display screen work, at regular intervals, and if they experience visual difficulties that may be due to display screen work; to an ophthalmological examination if needed; and to special corrective appliances if normal ones cannot be used. These measures may not involve workers in additional financial cost.

blocks.text: The Annex adds a requirement that is easy to miss in training: in the operator and computer interface, "no quantitative or qualitative checking facility may be used without the knowledge of the workers". Where software monitors keystrokes or output, workers must know about it, and the information duty in Article 6(1) is a natural place to record that they were told.

sections.heading: What evidence shows compliance with Article 6?

blocks.text: Good evidence shows the trigger, the content, and the link to the worker's own workstation. The table maps each obligation to the roles it applies to, the frequency, and the evidence an inspector would expect.

blocks.text: Recording the workstation analysis and the training against the same worker and location makes the link auditable. The approach in [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) applies directly.

sections.heading: How should an organization build display screen training?

blocks.text: Build it around the worker's own workstation and the employer's analysis, not around general ergonomics. A practical sequence follows.

items: Identify covered workers using the Article 2(c) test and any national threshold, and record the basis for the decision.
Complete or update the Article 3 analysis for each workstation type, including home or hybrid workstations if national law brings them into scope.
Train each worker before screen work starts, with a practical check that they can adjust their chair, screen, and lighting to the Annex standard.
Explain break arrangements, the eye test entitlement, and how to report discomfort or visual difficulty.
Define what counts as a substantial modification and attach retraining to that change process.

blocks.text: Office ergonomics often sits beside psychosocial risk, since Article 3 names mental stress. Related obligations are covered in [psychosocial hazards training requirements](/regulations/psychosocial-hazards-training-requirements), and EU-OSHA's [summary of Directive 90/270/EEC](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directives/5) links to the Commission's 2017 evaluation of how the directive is implemented in practice.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry structures workstation knowledge as concepts tied to the Annex requirements and to the employer's workstation analysis, with practical assessment points such as correct chair and screen adjustment. When a workstation is substantially modified, the affected workers and the concepts they need retrained on can be identified from those links.

faqs.q: How often must display screen training be repeated?
faqs.a: The directive sets no interval. Article 6(2) requires training before display screen work starts and whenever the organization of the workstation is substantially modified. National transposing laws or the employer's risk assessment may add a refresh cycle, and the rationale should be recorded.

faqs.q: Does the directive apply to laptops?
faqs.a: It excludes only "portable" systems not in prolonged use at a workstation. A laptop used for prolonged periods at a workstation is not excluded, so the workstation requirements, training, and eye test entitlement apply to the worker using it, subject to the national transposing law.

faqs.q: Who pays for eye tests and glasses for screen work?
faqs.a: Article 9(4) states that measures under that article "may in no circumstances involve workers in additional financial cost". Special corrective appliances are required only where tests show they are necessary and normal ones cannot be used. Article 9(5) allows eye protection to be provided through a national health system.

faqs.q: Does a hybrid or remote worker need this training?
faqs.a: The directive applies to covered workers at their workstation and does not mention home working, which was rare in 1990. Whether a home workstation falls within national rules depends on the Member State's law, so check the transposing act and any national telework rules.
